title: Changes in Sea Surface Temperatures and Primary Productivity in the Northern Japan Sea Since the Pliocene
content:
Abstract

The Japan Sea is a marginal sea connected to the surrounding oceans only through four shallow straits. It is a natural archive of the changes in ocean currents associated with the formation of the Japanese archipelago and variations in the Asian monsoon. However, the long-term response of the surface layer in the Japan Sea to tectonic movements and global environmental events remains unclear. We analyzed algal and terrestrial plant biomarkers in sediment cores from Integrated Ocean Drilling Program (IODP) Site U1423 (the northern Japan Sea off Hokkaido) to reconstruct the variations in marine primary production and paleoenvironmental changes since the Pliocene (∼4 Ma). The alkenone-based SSTs displayed a cooling trend after the Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (NHG), with significant cooling at 1.7 Ma due to the strengthening of the East Asian Winter Monsoon (EAWM), which was possibly related to the strengthening of the halocline in the North Pacific and the emergence of the Cold Tongue in the eastern equatorial Pacific (EEP). After 1.2 Ma, the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) reached the area off Hokkaido and promoted the formation of Japan Sea Proper Water (JSPW). Furthermore, we reconstructed the north–south shifts of the position of the subpolar front in the Japan Sea controlled by the balance between the TWC and EAWM, and paleo-primary production based on alkenone and diol biomarkers, which were influenced by nutrient supply from upwelling and terrestrial input (traced by n-alkanes).
